Noyce IDE is a desktop IDE built on Code-OSS, the open-source core of Visual Studio Code. You edit firmware in a normal editor, and next to it the IDE adds surfaces that each measure one kind of engineering evidence from the project you have open: Know the code: Project Graph, System Architecture, Semantic Search, and Register Knowledge, which indexes your microcontroller's reference manual and links its registers to the code that uses them, citing the page. Prove it: MISRA C diagnostics, CBMC formal verification, CodeQL code scanning, and measured MC/DC coverage. Trace it: requirements, the Traceability Graph, and the DO-178C Annex A objective model. Author and certify: the 17 DO-178C life-cycle documents, compliance runs, evidence records, a hash-chained audit trail and a certification package. Agents: an Orchestrator with 15 agents, plus an agents chat panel. Code changes from the Orchestrator and from Fix with Noyce are staged as change sets you approve before anything is written. Inline edits in the editor are previewed as a diff you accept or reject, and edits made from the chat can be reverted.

What you already have (left) is read by analysis engines on your machine. Every finding is recorded in .noyce/: in a hash-chained audit ledger and in compliance runs pinned to one commit. Those records are graded against the 71 DO-178C Annex A objectives, cited in your life-cycle documents and exported as a sealed package. Agents only draft; a person on your roster approves. Three ideas run through every page of these docs: Measured, or marked. A surface shows what a real tool measured on your project, or it says nothing was measured. Sample data is labelled and never counts. Agents draft, people decide. Agents write drafts, fixes and evidence. Nothing an agent produces satisfies an objective until a named person on your roster accepts it, and fixes from Fix with Noyce, the fixers and the Orchestrator reach your code only as change sets that a person approves. Everything lands in .noyce/. Results, records and documents live in one folder in the project, outside version control, and the important ones are hashed so changes are detectable.

Every screenshot in these docs was taken from the current build of Noyce IDE running on a copy of the Canister Main Controller firmware, a production TI Tiva TM4C1294 project. The numbers you see, such as 624 stored MISRA findings, 29 requirements and 71 Annex A objectives, are what the IDE measured on that copy. Empty states are shown as they are: where a tool has not been run, the screenshot says so. NoteThe copy includes uncommitted changes from earlier Noyce IDE sessions: @req and @verification comment blocks at the top of eight source files, and edits to a few functions. They are why the Annotation Navigator finds requirement tags. Nothing was written to the project to make these docs; Noyce IDE keeps what it generates in the project's .noyce/ folder. See The .noyce folder.

Noyce IDE ships as a desktop application built on Code-OSS. Pick your platform below. Everything Noyce IDE generates for a project stays inside that project's .noyce/ folder. Nothing is uploaded unless you point the IDE at a cloud model.

Choose one of the three methods. Homebrew is the easiest to keep up to date.

Add the Noyce tap, then install the cask: TerminalCopybrew tap Hitheshkaranth/noyce https://github.com/Hitheshkaranth/noyce_ide brew install --cask noyce-ide The cask installs Noyce IDE.app into /Applications and clears the macOS quarantine flag for you, so the app opens normally on first launch.

The script downloads the latest Apple silicon .dmg, copies the app into /Applications (replacing any previous copy), and clears the quarantine flag: TerminalCopycurl -fsSL https://raw.githubusercontent.com/Hitheshkaranth/noyce_ide/main/scripts/install/install.sh | bash

Download NoyceIDE-<version>-darwin-arm64.dmg for the latest version from the releases page. Open the disk image and drag Noyce IDE into Applications. Clear the quarantine flag before the first launch: TerminalCopyxattr -dr com.apple.quarantine "/Applications/Noyce IDE.app" WarningThe macOS build is ad-hoc signed and not notarized. If you skip step 3, macOS reports that the app "is damaged" or comes from an unidentified developer and refuses to open it. Homebrew and the one-line installer run this step for you.

Download NoyceIDE-<version>-win32-x64-system-<commit>.exe for the latest version from the releases page. Run the installer. It installs for all users, so Windows asks for administrator approval. If Microsoft Defender SmartScreen shows Windows protected your PC, select More info, then Run anyway. WarningThe Windows installer is not code-signed yet, which is why SmartScreen warns. Windows support is in beta.

Open Noyce IDE from Applications or the Start menu. The Noyce IDE tab opens with Open folder…, Import project… and New project, your recent projects, and a tile for every workbench surface. Continue with the Quick start. The start tab after opening the Canister Main Controller firmware (TI Tiva TM4C1294).

Noyce IDE runs without any of these. Each one switches on a specific kind of evidence; when a tool is missing, the surface that needs it says so and nothing is faked. OCR for schematics is bundled as well. If the STM32 tools are installed somewhere Noyce IDE does not search, point it at them in Settings: Setting Points to noyce.stm32.cubeIdePath The STM32CubeIDE install folder, for example /Applications/STM32CubeIDE.app or C:\ST\STM32CubeIDE_1.15.0. Its bundled make, GNU tools, STM32CubeProgrammer, ST-LINK GDB server, OpenOCD and headless builder are then used. The standard install locations are searched without this. noyce.stm32.armToolchainPath A folder holding arm-none-eabi-gcc and arm-none-eabi-gdb. Used by Validate Toolchain, the generated build tasks and the debug launch. Run Validate Toolchain afterwards to see what was found. NoteIf GCC and gcov are installed but LLVM is not, coverage still reports statements and branches, and MC/DC reads "MC/DC unavailable" with the reason. gcov cannot measure MC/DC at any version.
The AI features need a model. Noyce IDE starts pointed at LM Studio on http://localhost:1234; any OpenAI-compatible server (vLLM included) works the same way. See Models.

Homebrew: brew upgrade --cask noyce-ide One-line installer: run the same command again; it replaces the app with the latest release. Disk image or Windows: download and run the newer release. There is no in-app updater. Your settings and every project's .noyce/ folder are kept across updates.

TerminalCopy# Homebrew: remove the app brew uninstall --cask noyce-ide # or remove the app and its settings brew uninstall --zap --cask noyce-ide # extensions and per-user data live here, and are not removed by --zap rm -rf ~/.noyce-ide If you installed from the disk image or the one-line installer, drag /Applications/Noyce IDE.app to the Bin, then delete ~/Library/Application Support/Noyce IDE and ~/.noyce-ide if you want your settings gone too.

Open Settings → Apps → Installed apps, find Noyce IDE, and choose Uninstall. Settings stay in %APPDATA%\Noyce IDE and extensions in %USERPROFILE%\.noyce-ide; delete those folders to remove everything. TipUninstalling never touches your projects. Each project's generated evidence stays in its own .noyce/ folder until you delete it.
This walkthrough uses the screenshots from a real project, the Canister Main Controller firmware (TI Tiva TM4C1294, Code Composer Studio). Any C firmware project works the same way.
Install Noyce IDE. Optional: connect a model. Steps 1 to 4 below work without one. Optional: install cppcheck for full MISRA analysis (brew install cppcheck on macOS).

On the Noyce IDE start tab, choose one of: Open folder… opens any folder as it is. Import project… starts the import wizard; Import and build follows it through for a TI and an ST project. Pick Code Composer Studio (.ccsproject), STM32CubeIDE (.ioc), MPLAB X (nbproject) or Generic Folder. The wizard detects the microcontroller and, when it recognises an ST or TI part, downloads that part's reference manual in the background and indexes it for Register Knowledge. That download needs a network connection; everything else works offline. The start tab. The project actions at the top, then recent projects, then a tile for each of the 29 surfaces. NoteUse the Import Project button on the start tab. The Command Palette entry Noyce: Import Project only picks a folder and does not run the wizard. Opening a project creates a .noyce/ folder inside it for everything Noyce IDE generates. Its life-cycle data is meant to be committed with the project; its own .gitignore keeps out the caches and scratch files. See The .noyce folder.

Press ⌘⌥N then S (CtrlAltN then S on Windows), or run Noyce Compliance: Scan Workspace. Noyce IDE finds every @req and @verification tag in your source, shows the counts, and opens the Annotation Navigator. Annotation Navigator on the Canister firmware: 20 tags, each with its file, line and comment text. ImportantA tag is not evidence. The navigator labels a requirement Verified only when an executed test result backs it; tagged requirements without one read Needs review. The Compliance Dashboard shows the verified count, which on this project reads 0 of 29. If your code has no tags yet, that is fine. Requirements can also come from documents and imports; see Requirements & traceability.

Open MISRA Diagnostics from its tile, or run Noyce Compliance: Open MISRA Diagnostics, then select Scan. Findings are grouped by severity (Mandatory, Required, Advisory) and by the tool that reported them. Select a finding to see its rule, file and line, with Open in Editor and Fix with Noyce. Static Analysis on the Canister firmware: 624 stored findings, filterable by severity and tool. The detail pane offers Open in Editor and Fix with Noyce. ImportantFindings from the built-in heuristic scan are labelled not evidence. Only findings from a real analyzer (cppcheck with the MISRA addon, or clang-tidy) count toward compliance.

Open Compliance (⌘⌥N then C). The Compliance Dashboard grades the project against DO-178C and shows each Annex A objective with the evidence behind it. Compliance Evidence for the Canister firmware: 0 of 29 requirements linked, 1,532 analysis findings, and 71 objectives: 29 partial, 42 open, none satisfied. An objective is only satisfied when its own evidence exists and a person has reviewed it. On a project that has just been opened, most objectives read open or partial; that is the honest starting point, not an error.

Every AI feature in Noyce IDE, including the Orchestrator agents, Fix with Noyce, document authoring and Semantic Search, runs through the model you configure on the AI Models page. Noyce IDE can run fully offline against a model on your own machine or LAN. Open it with Noyce AI: Open AI Models from the Command Palette (⇧⌘P on macOS, Ctrl+Shift+P on Windows). AI Models: the catalog on the left; endpoint, generation parameters, embeddings, concurrency and agent role assignment on the right.

Chat requests from agents, Fix with Noyce and document authoring go to the global model, or to the model assigned to that agent role. Embedding requests from Semantic Search go to the embedding server, which must serve an embedding model and can be a different machine. There are two separate kinds of request, and they can go to different servers: Chat (generating text and code) goes to the global model you select, unless that agent role has its own model. Embeddings (turning text into vectors for Semantic Search) go to the server set under Embeddings. A server that only serves a chat model cannot answer them.

sections.h: Use a local server (LM Studio, vLLM)
sections.t: Start the server and load a model. For LM Studio, enable its local server. In AI Models, select Loaded model (auto-detect) in the Model Catalog, or pick a specific model. Under Server URL (LM Studio, vLLM, or any OpenAI-compatible server), enter the address, for example http://localhost:1234 or http://<host>:8000 for vLLM. A trailing /v1 is accepted. Leave API key empty unless the server was started with --api-key. The key is stored in the operating system keychain and sent only to that server. TipIf the server does not report the model's context length, set Context window (tokens) for that model. Noyce IDE sizes every prompt to fit it.

Choose the provider in the catalog and paste its key into the matching field (Google API Key, Anthropic API Key, OpenAI API Key or OpenRouter API Key). WarningCloud API keys are stored in the operating system keychain, like the local-server key and the per-agent keys. Prefer a local model for proprietary firmware, and switch on Classified in the status bar to have the IDE refuse every cloud provider, including from the agents chat and the hosted CLIs.

Semantic Search and agent grounding need an embedding model. Set it in AI Models → Embeddings: Embedding server: the same server as chat, Ollama, LM Studio / vLLM, or OpenAI. Embedding model: defaults to text-embedding-nomic-embed-text-v1.5 on LM Studio, nomic-embed-text on Ollama, and text-embedding-3-small on OpenAI. Select Save & test. Noyce IDE sends one request and reports the vector size it got back. If you change the embedding model, rebuild the Semantic Search index.

Orchestrator Concurrency sets how many agent calls run at once. It defaults to 3 for local servers and 1 for hosted APIs. Agent Role Assignment gives any of the 15 Orchestrator agents its own model. An agent left on Global default uses the model selected above. Generation Parameters (temperature and max tokens) are shared defaults for global model runs. The Fixer model select in MISRA Diagnostics overrides the model for Fix with Noyce only.

sections.t: Two real projects, imported into a fresh copy and taken as far as this computer allows. Every step and screenshot below was checked in the IDE: a TI Tiva TM4C1294 project from Code Composer Studio; an STM32G431 project from STM32CubeIDE. Both end in a passing, linked build. The STM32 project first needed two things fixed, and both were reported by the IDE: a compiler without its C library, and makefiles generated on another computer. Both problems and their fixes are shown.

For You need Importing either kind Nothing beyond Noyce IDE. The reference-manual download needs a network connection. Building a TI project The TI ARM compiler (armcl, TI Arm Clang or GNU Arm), and TivaWare when the project uses it. Noyce IDE finds them on your PATH or under ~/ti, /Applications/ti, C:\ti or %USERPROFILE%\ti. See Build. Building an STM32 project make and a complete Arm GNU Toolchain, that is arm-none-eabi-gcc with its C library (newlib). STM32CubeIDE's bundled toolchain or the Arm GNU Toolchain both work. Prefer the GCC version the project declares (see step 4). Flashing and debugging an STM32 arm-none-eabi-gdb, plus OpenOCD, STM32CubeProgrammer or st-util. TipTry this on a copy of your project first. The import itself writes only .noyce/, but the STM32 workspace step (step 3 of the STM32 walkthrough) writes .vscode/ files and overwrites files of the same names.

Choose Yes, I trust the authors; in Restricted Mode, Code-OSS does not run tasks, so the builds below would not start. A Project Imported notification appears. Noyce IDE detects the microcontroller from the project's files and fetches its reference manual for Register Knowledge. A notification reports the outcome: Reference manual indexed: the PDF is in .noyce/manuals/ and its register index in .noyce/knowledge/. Reference manual for the part, as a warning: the download failed. The message names the manual and its URL, so you can download it in a browser and choose it with Choose PDF… in Register Knowledge. A server that does not answer is abandoned after 30 seconds. The project is added to Recent projects on the start tab, marked Current. The import writes only the .noyce/ folder, including its .gitignore for caches and the downloaded manuals. See The .noyce folder.

sections.h: Walkthrough: a TivaWare project from Code Composer Studio
sections.t: The project: an MPDU controller on a TM4C1294NCPDT, built with TI ARM CGT 20.2.6.LTS and TivaWare 2.2.0.295, both installed under ~/ti.

Import project… → Code Composer Studio → the project folder. After the reload and the trust prompt, the reference-manual notification reports that the TM4C1294 datasheet (spms433.pdf) was downloaded and indexed.

The status bar now shows the configuration (Debug) and Build. Press ⇧⌘B (CtrlShiftB on Windows). The build runs as the Noyce: Build Debug task in the terminal. When it finishes, the status bar reads Built 12.7s, and its warnings are in the Problems panel. The objects, .out and .map are written to .noyce/build/ccs-Debug/, not to the project's own Debug/ folder.

sections.h: 3. Read the result in the Build view
sections.t: Open the Build Pipeline tile, or ⌘⌥N then B. The Build view after the ⇧⌘B build: the compiler and version in the header, the counts, the image size from the link map, and every warning with its TI diagnostic code and file:line. The header names the compiler that was found and its version. Image size comes from the link map. Diagnostics lists each warning with its TI code (994-D, 179-D…); select a file and line to open it. See The Build view for the other tabs.

Select Open Firmware Memory. Firmware Memory reads the TI linker map the build wrote under .noyce/build: each region against its budget, its sections, and what each object file costs. Firmware Memory finds the map the build wrote and shows each memory region against its size, with its sections and the cost of each object file. On this project, SRAM is 106.0 KB of 256 KB and FLASH is 54.6 KB of 1 MB. Worst case stack depth stays —: it needs GCC -fstack-usage records, which a TI build does not produce. The configured .stack size (2.0 KB) is still shown.

sections.h: 5. Rebuild the pin map from the source
sections.t: A CCS project has no .ioc, so the pin configuration is reconstructed from the TivaWare calls in the C source (GPIOPinConfigure, GPIOPinType…, SysCtlPeripheralEnable). To run it and open the result, use Noyce Tiva: Import Pin Config from Source from the Command Palette. In the folder picker, choose the project folder (the open folder is preselected). The TM4C1294NCPDT in its TQFP128 package, rebuilt from the TivaWare source. The peripherals the source enables (UART0, UART1, UART4…) are switched on. The Pin Configurator opens on the part and package detected from the source. The peripherals the source configures are switched on, and each pin is coloured by its use. Generate init code writes initialisation code for the configuration shown. See Pin Configurator.
The project: an H-bridge controller on an STM32G431VBTx, last built in STM32CubeIDE on a Windows machine.

Import project… → STM32CubeIDE → the project's .ioc file. After the reload and the trust prompt: the .ioc opens in the Pin Configurator, with the part, the package and the peripherals the .ioc enables; the reference manual (RM0440 for the STM32G4) is fetched. In the run shown here, st.com did not answer, so the warning gave the manual's URL to download by hand. The STM32G431VBTx in LQFP100, opened from the .ioc: ADC1, DMA, GPIO, RCC, TIM3/4/6 and USART1–3 enabled.

Run Noyce STM32: Validate Toolchain. The Noyce STM32 output lists each tool, then whether you can build, flash and debug, and why not. First run: the build is blocked because Homebrew's arm-none-eabi-gcc has no C library, and flash and debug are blocked because no flash tool, GDB or GDB server is installed. On the first run here, all three were blocked: Build: the arm-none-eabi-gcc on PATH was Homebrew's formula, which has no C library (nano.specs and libc.a are missing). Flash: no STM32CubeProgrammer, OpenOCD or st-util, so no flash task is generated. Debug: no arm-none-eabi-gdb and no GDB server. The fix for the build is a complete toolchain, and a setting that points at it: Install the Arm GNU Toolchain, or use the one inside STM32CubeIDE. Arm's macOS .tar.xz downloads unpack anywhere with no installer, for example into ~/tools/. Set noyce.stm32.armToolchainPath to its bin folder, for example ~/tools/arm-gnu-toolchain-12.3.rel1-darwin-arm64-arm-none-eabi/bin. A toolchain in that folder wins over any copy on PATH, including a broken one. The setting is used by Validate Toolchain, the generated tasks (which put the folder first on their PATH), the debug launch, and the Build view. Run Validate Toolchain again: it lists arm-none-eabi-gcc and arm-none-eabi-gdb from the folder, and the newlib block is gone.

Run Noyce STM32: Regenerate Workspace Files. It writes .vscode/tasks.json, launch.json, settings.json, extensions.json and compile_commands.json for the open folder: a make build task, STM32 Build (Debug), which becomes the ⇧⌘B build; a flash task, when a flash tool was found; a Cortex-Debug launch configuration; clangd set up for the project. Noyce STM32: Import CubeIDE Project does the same after asking for the .ioc or project folder.

The Build view checks the CubeIDE makefiles first. Local paths: it runs make in Debug/. A path from another computer: the build is blocked until you regenerate the makefiles or build with a generated makefile. Either way the compiler comes from noyce.stm32.armToolchainPath, then PATH, then STM32CubeIDE, and one without a C library blocks the build. The build depends on the makefiles STM32CubeIDE generated in Debug/. Those makefiles hold absolute paths from the computer that generated them. With ⇧⌘B. The task runs make -j4 all in Debug/. Here, the makefiles named C:/… paths, so make stopped with makefile:63: *** multiple target patterns. Stop. The task's description in tasks.json warns about this when it is generated. The build is still recorded in Build Status, with the compiler version. From the Build view. The view checks the makefiles before running them. Because they name paths that do not exist on this computer, Build is disabled and Build blocked names one such path. It gives two ways out: Regenerate the makefiles: run the STM32 CubeIDE Headless Build task (it needs STM32CubeIDE installed), or build once in STM32CubeIDE on this computer. Build with a generated makefile: Noyce IDE writes its own makefile from the .cproject and .ioc, under .noyce/build/stm32-<configuration>/portable-build/. It then builds with make and the arm-none-eabi-gcc from noyce.stm32.armToolchainPath, or from PATH when the setting is empty. This is not the CubeIDE build, so check its output against a CubeIDE build before you rely on it. The CubeIDE makefiles stay blocked, but the generated-makefile build passed with Arm GNU Toolchain 12.3. Image size is read from its link map. Here, the generated-makefile build passed in 3.3 s with 10 warnings, and linked the .elf, .hex, .bin and .map. Image size is read from the new map. The Toolchain tab and the build record name the compiler and its measured version. ImportantUse the compiler version the project was built with. This project declares GNU Tools for STM32 12.3. With Arm GNU Toolchain 15.2, the same build stopped with one error, in a call to HAL_CRC_Calculate that passes a uint8_t * where the HAL declares uint32_t *. Since GCC 14, an incompatible pointer type is an error by default instead of a warning. The fault is in the source, but switching compilers mid-project changes what builds. Use the declared version, and fix such warnings deliberately. Along the way, a build that fails before the compiler reports any error against a file and line (for example, a compiler without newlib) shows Errors 0 with Failed before any located error; see Output. The Output tab starts with a one-line hint when the cause is a missing C library.

sections.h: 5. See where the memory and stack go
sections.t: Select Open Firmware Memory. It opens on the map the build just wrote under .noyce/build/. An older map in the project's own Debug/ folder stays in the picker, but is not chosen first. The generated build compiles with -fstack-usage, so Firmware Memory adds stack checks: worst-case depth along the deepest call path from main, against the linker's heap/stack reservation. Because the generated makefile compiles with -fstack-usage, this view adds what the TI build could not: Stack checks: the worst-case stack depth (288 B here), along the deepest path from main; whether that depth fits the linker's 1 KB reservation, and the space below it. The figures cover the functions with stack data (82.7 % here). The view states what each check does and does not establish.

Every recorded build is listed in Build Status in the Noyce IDE sidebar, newest first. Hover a build to see what ran (CubeIDE makefile, Generated makefile or CubeIDE headless) and its toolchain. Select it to open the Build view. Build Status lists every STM32 build of this walkthrough, newest first: the failed ⇧⌘B runs and the generated-makefile builds, failed and then passed. Beside it, the generated tasks.json and the terminal where make stopped on a C: path.

Quick start: scan the imported project for requirement annotations and run static analysis. Hardware: Register Knowledge from the downloaded manual, probes, RTT and the serial monitor. Build, test & debug: build configurations, your own build tasks, the test explorer and the firmware validation loop.

This guide follows the path Noyce IDE lays out in the Compliance Run view: plans and standards, requirements, design, code, verification, then the summaries. Noyce IDE does the measuring and drafting. People do the deciding: every objective is closed by a named reviewer on your roster, never by an AI. ImportantNoyce IDE produces evidence and drafts. It does not certify software. Your certification authority and DER decide what is acceptable. 01THE DAL PATHthe order the Compliance Run view lays outPlans & standardsPSAC · SDP · SVP …A-1RequirementsSRS · HLRA-2 · A-3DesignSDD · LLRA-4CodeMISRA · CodeQLA-5Verificationtests · CBMC · MC/DCA-6 · A-7SummariesSVR SCI SECI SASA-8 – A-10Compliance runevery producer, one commitCertification packagesealed, ledger-anchoredAT EVERY STAGE agents draft → a person on the roster reviews, accepts and signsSVR and SAS cannot be issued until a compliance run shows executed verification. The DAL path. Each stage covers its Annex A tables, as the Compliance Run view tags them. A compliance run measures every stage at one commit and feeds the certification package. At every stage, agents draft and a person on the roster reviews, accepts and signs. The stages are ordered because each one is checked against the one before: requirements against the plans, design against the requirements, code against the design, and verification against all of them. You can work on several at once; the Compliance Run view shows each stage's progress and suggests the next action for it.

Open the project and connect a model. Document authoring and agent drafting need a model; the measurements do not. Open Compliance (⌘⌥N then C) and set the framework to DO-178C and the assurance level to your DAL in the header selects. The level is saved with the project's compliance article and printed on document covers. Open Evidence Records → Roster and add every person who will review, approve or sign. Reviews, approvals and signatures can only be recorded against people on the roster. LimitationSet the DAL on the Compliance Dashboard. The Assurance Level in Settings → Compliance Standards is not saved and has no effect. The Compliance Run, Certification Readiness, Coupling and MC/DC views currently assess against Level A regardless of the level you pick.

sections.h: 1. Import the Annex A table you are licensed to use
sections.t: The wording of the DO-178C Annex A objectives belongs to RTCA, so Noyce IDE does not ship it. Until you import your licensed copy, plans and summaries are marked DRAFT, not for submission. On the Compliance Dashboard, expand Licensed Annex A table. Select Write blank template. Noyce IDE writes .noyce/compliance/annex-a-licensed.template.json. Fill in applicability, independence and control category for your level, and save it as annex-a-licensed.json in the same folder. Objective text for the run view is imported separately in Compliance Run → Objective map → Import objective text.

Open DO-178C Documents. The library holds all 17 life-cycle documents, grouped as Plans (PSAC, SDP, SVP, SCMP, SQAP), Standards (SRSTD, SDSTD, SCSTD), Core (SRS, SDD, ICD, TRACE), Verification (SVCP, SVR) and Summary (SECI, SCI, SAS). DO-178C Documents on the Canister firmware: each document's card shows its revision and whether it is baselined. For each plan: Select Create from template. Sections that can be filled from the workspace, such as the toolchain, the file list and the target, are filled immediately, without a model. PSAC fills most of its sections this way. Select Propose decisions. An agent drafts each section that needs engineering judgment and marks it PROPOSED, awaiting engineer review. Nothing proposed counts until a person accepts it. Open Review decisions. For each draft choose Accept, Edit and accept, or Reject with a comment the next draft must answer. Each acceptance is recorded as a review in the audit trail. Optionally select Run docs swarm (or Author set… for several documents) to have agents write the remaining prose. Each section is saved as it is written, so a stopped run resumes where it left off. To use your company's Word template, select Document template… → Import from .docx. Noyce IDE lifts the styles, header, footer, page setup and logo, and applies them to every export.

High-level requirements live in the SRS. Bring them in from wherever they are today: Requirements Authoring: write HLRs directly, or import system requirements from CSV, ReqIF or a Markdown table. A live check blocks the reviewed status on statements with two "shall"s, a TBD, or no parent. Source tags: @req and @verification comments in code are picked up by Scan Workspace. Low-Level Requirements: drafts one LLR per function from the code. A draft counts only once a person on the roster accepts it. See Requirements & traceability for each view.

System Architecture builds a C4 model from the code and exports it for the SDD. MISRA Diagnostics reports coding-standard findings. Fix them with Fix with Noyce, record a MISRA deviation, or leave them open; each fix becomes a change set you approve. See Review AI changes. Code Scanning (CodeQL) and Formal Verification (CBMC) add security and proof evidence.

Test Explorer finds the project's tests and records target test runs. MC/DC Coverage measures statement, decision and MC/DC coverage with LLVM, per module. Data & Control Coupling and Object Code Traceability cover DO-178C A-7(8) and A-7(9). Record each review in Evidence Records → Reviews. Independence is worked out from who wrote the item and who reviewed it; you do not tick a box. A review by an AI, a self-review, or a review by someone not on the roster is never independent.

Open Compliance Run and select Take a run. Noyce IDE runs every evidence producer against the current commit and stores the result as a reproducible record. Compliance Run: no run recorded yet on this copy. The DAL path below lists what each stage still needs. The run shows, per Annex A table, which objectives are evidenced, unmapped or still open, what each tool reported, and what changed since the previous run. Map producers to objectives with Objective map → Map…; every mapping needs a stated basis. Select Mark baseline to fix a run as your reference. Here is a real first run on the Canister copy: Run run-20261023-100235 on the Canister copy: 0 of 71 objectives evidenced, 6 of 15 producers ran, 6 failing measurements, 1 of 8 conformity questions answered. Its Configuration section records commit 8ee50f2, a dirty working tree and level DO-178C A, and lists the 16 reasons export is blocked. Read a first run like this one as a to-do list, not a verdict. Each of the 16 Blocks export lines names a concrete gap and usually the fix: documents not yet baselined, requirements with no parent, a static analyzer that is not registered as a qualified tool, CodeQL include paths that could not be resolved, CBMC that ran on seeded sample input, and a working tree with uncommitted changes. The DAL path above it tells you which stage to work on next. A run cannot be exported if a producer failed, sample data was used, there is no commit, or the working tree has uncommitted changes.

In each document's Completion tab, resolve what is left: proposals awaiting review, engineering decisions, evidence the workspace has not produced yet, and cross-document consistency. Then choose the signatories from the roster and select Sign and issue (baseline). The issued revision is frozen with a SHA-256 content hash. SVR and SAS cannot be issued until the latest compliance run shows executed verification. When the whole set is ready, select Declare set baseline in the library; it records the git commit. Select Export .docx on any document for a Word copy with your template, numbered headings, tables and figures.

On the Compliance Dashboard, select Certification Package. Noyce IDE runs CBMC and CodeQL, gathers the requirements, traceability, analysis, coverage, reviews, documents and audit trail, and writes Markdown, HTML and JSON to .noyce/certification/. The button stays disabled until there are requirements and every objective has been assessed or reviewed, and the export is refused while the document set has unwaived contradictions. NoteThe package is sealed, not signed. Each section is hashed with SHA-256, and the package digest is anchored to the head of the hash-chained audit trail, so any later change is detectable. It carries no private-key signature.

sections.h: How Annex A objectives are graded
sections.t: Status Meaning Satisfied The objective's own evidence exists and a person has reviewed it. Partial Some of the objective's evidence exists, or a project-wide measure suggests progress. A proxy can make an objective partial, never satisfied. Open / unassessed No mapped evidence yet. This is "not shown", not "failed". Failing A check that maps to the objective failed.

Code changes proposed by AI in Noyce IDE are never written straight into your source. They arrive as a change set: the proposed files, held next to the project, that have to cite an authority, pass gates and be approved by a named person before they are applied. This applies to Fix with Noyce in MISRA Diagnostics, the fixers in Formal Verification and Code Scanning, the Firmware Validation Loop, and code written by Orchestrator agents. 01PROPOSED02STAGEDheld beside the project, not written03DECIDED BY A PERSONFix with NoyceMISRA findingCBMC · CodeQL fixersfailed property, alertOrchestrator agentscode tasksFirmware loopbuild-fix attemptsChange setfiles + diffCite authorityopen PR or CCBRun gatesintegrityauthority · buildunit tests · MISRAall five always runApproveapprover on rosterApplyall files or nonefile changed since gatingStalenothing writtenor rejectRejectedreason recordedBefore staging, Fix with Noyce asks the model whether the finding is real; a disputed finding cannot be staged. Every AI code change takes the same path. It is staged beside the project, cites the authority that allows it, runs five gates, and is approved by a person on the roster before Apply writes all of its files or none. If a file changed after gating, the set goes stale and nothing is written; a rejection always records its reason. The point of the path is that the code an auditor sees can always be traced back to a reason (the authority), a check (the gates) and a person (the approver). An AI wrote the draft; none of those three steps are the AI's.

In MISRA Diagnostics, select a finding, then Fix with Noyce. The dialog shows Generating a grounded fix… while the model works. What happens before you see a diff: Fact check. The model is first asked whether the finding is a real violation. A disputed finding cannot be staged, and the dialog says why. A bounded rewrite. The model rewrites only a window around the finding: the enclosing function when it is short, otherwise about 25 lines either side. The rest of the file is kept byte for byte, so a fix cannot silently change code far from the finding. Safety checks on the result. If the proposal changes nothing, or would damage the file, staging is disabled and the dialog says so. When the proposal is a real change, the dialog shows its line diff: each changed line with three lines around it, and the unchanged stretches of the file folded. Select a folded row to show those lines. Select Stage change set to keep the proposal, Discard to drop it, or Raise problem report from finding to track the issue instead. Fix All stages one change set for every auto-fixable finding. A real run with Ornith on the Canister copy. cppcheck reports that line 159 of CANISTER_CONTROLLER_INIT.c copies four bytes into MAIN_SYS_DATA->HOST_id, a two-byte field. The proposal bounds the copy to the field's size: that stops the overflow, but it stores only "FC" of "FCCU", and the explanation gets the field sizes wrong. This is why a person reviews every proposal against the code before staging it. A proposal can be well-formed and still wrong. Read the diff against the code it changes, not against the explanation. TipPick the model for fixes in the Fixer model select at the top of MISRA Diagnostics. It overrides the global model for fixes only.

Open Evidence Records → Change sets. Each staged set shows its files with a per-file diff. Evidence Records. Change sets is one of ten record types; the others hold verification cases, problem reports, reviews and more.

Every change needs a reason that a reviewer can trace. In Authority, enter the problem report, change request or CCB decision the change answers, and select Cite. If none exists yet, Raise problem report from finding creates one.

Select Run gates. All five gates always run, so you see every problem at once: Gate Passes when Integrity The changed files have no structural damage a compiler would reject, such as an unbalanced brace or a stray byte-order mark. Problems already in the original file are listed but do not fail the gate. Authority The cited problem report is open or in work, or a CCB decision taken with quorum approved the change. Build The project builds with the change. Unit tests The project's tests pass with the change. If they also fail without it, the result says so. MISRA The change introduces no new MISRA findings. A gate that cannot run is marked skipped, never passed: for example when the project has no portable build, no unit tests the IDE can run, or no C or C++ file in the change. Gating refuses to start if the staged content was edited outside the change set.

Choose the Approver from the roster and select Approve. Then select Apply. Apply writes all of the files or none of them. If any file was edited after the gates ran, the change set is marked stale and nothing is written; propose the fix again on the current code. If a write fails part-way, the files already written are restored. To decline a change, enter a reason and select Reject; a rejection always records its reason. Every step (creation, cited authority, gate results, approval, rejection, apply) is kept in the change set's history.

Code from the Orchestrator's coding agents goes through the same path. With Auto-apply agent code off, the agent output tab shows Proposed file changes with Stage all as change set. With it on, the change set is staged for you automatically. In both cases nothing is written until you approve and apply it here.

The Noyce IDE tab opens when the IDE starts. Reopen it any time with ⌘⌥N then D, or Noyce: Show Getting Started. The start tab on the Canister copy: the project actions and keyboard starters at the top, your recent projects, and a tile for each of the 29 surfaces. Open folder… opens any folder as a project. Import project… starts the import wizard (below). New project opens Project Templates. On a wide window, the keyboard shortcuts for a build, the Compliance Dashboard, the Test Explorer and the Command Palette sit beside them. Recent projects lists what you opened before. Workbench surfaces has a tile per surface, grouped by area; type in Filter surfaces to narrow them. Each tile opens its surface in its own editor tab, so you can arrange surfaces side by side like files. New Project and Try the demo open demonstration content only; see Known limitations.

The Import Project wizard understands four kinds of project: Type Recognised by Code Composer Studio (TI) .ccsproject STM32CubeIDE (ST) .ioc MPLAB X (Microchip) nbproject/ Generic folder Any folder of C sources The wizard analyses the project, opens it, and detects the microcontroller. Import and build walks through a TI and an ST import step by step. For a recognised ST or TI part it then downloads that part's reference manual and indexes it for Register Knowledge. The download runs in the background and needs a network connection.

Noyce STM32: Import CubeIDE Project generates .vscode/launch.json and compile_commands.json for an STM32CubeIDE project, set up for OpenOCD. Noyce Tiva: Import Pin Config from Source rebuilds the pin map of a TivaWare project from its C source. Opening an .ioc file opens it straight in the Pin Configurator. Validate Toolchain checks that the Arm GNU tools, debugger and OpenOCD are on your PATH.

Noyce IDE keeps the Code-OSS layout you may know from Visual Studio Code, and adds: Activity bar icons for Noyce IDE, Compliance, Hardware, Noyce AI, Project Graph and Architecture. Each opens views in the sidebar: Icon View Shows Noyce IDE Noyce Tools Every tool, grouped into Development, Hardware, Test & Telemetry, and Safety & Collaboration. Select one to open it. Build Status The 10 most recent builds of the project, TI CCS or STM32CubeIDE, newest first, with the result, the kind, the duration and the time. Hover one for the toolchain and exit code; select it to open the Build view. See Where the output goes. Project Lifecycle Project Templates, Build Pipeline, Team Activity, Review Workflow and Audit Log. STM32 Debug State The attached probe, core registers and your memory watches. See Hardware. Compliance Compliance Every compliance surface, from the Dashboard to Scan Workspace. Hardware Hardware Every hardware surface. Serial Ports The serial ports on this machine, checked every 10 seconds. Select one to open it in the Serial Monitor. Noyce AI Noyce AI AI Orchestrator, Run Agent Pipeline, Agents Chat and AI Models. Project Graph, Architecture Selecting the icon opens the Project Graph or System Architecture in the editor. Agents in the secondary sidebar: the agents chat and its history. Status bar items: the Classified mode toggle, the CodeGraph symbol count, the Noyce IDE service status (Noyce: ok), the number of serial ports (No Ports when there are none; select it to open the Serial Monitor), and the AI activity with its live token rate. The Compliance launcher lists every compliance surface with a one-line description. Every surface can also be opened from the Command Palette. See Commands & shortcuts.

Switch on Classified in the status bar when the project's source must not leave your machine. While it is on, every call to a cloud model provider is refused: from the Noyce IDE window, from the agents chat panel, and from the hosted Claude, Codex and Gemini CLIs. Local models keep working; see Connect a model.

Noyce IDE builds one requirements picture from three sources: requirements you write or import, @req and @verification tags in source code, and the requirements sections of your DO-178C documents. The register, the graphs and the Compliance Dashboard all read the same picture. 01SOURCES02ONE REQUIREMENTS PICTURE03WHERE YOU SEE ITRequirements AuthoringHLRs → SRS-001 · CSV / ReqIF / MarkdownSource tags@req · @verification in commentsLow-level requirementsdrafted per function, accepted by a personRequirements + trace linkssystem → HLR → LLR → code → testrebuilt when .noyce/requirements changesRequirements & Evidencethe registerTraceability Graphlinks, liveCompliance DashboardA-2 … A-7 objectivesTruth Graphunresolved referencesaccepted LLRs generateCBMC harnessesstaged as a change set Requirements written or imported in Requirements Authoring, @req and @verification tags in source, and accepted low-level requirements form one picture with its trace links. The register, the Traceability Graph, the Compliance Dashboard and the Truth Graph all read it, and accepted low-level requirements also generate CBMC harnesses. Because there is one picture, fixing a trace gap in any view fixes it everywhere. If the register and the dashboard ever disagree, rescan: the graph is rebuilt whenever the files in .noyce/requirements/ or .noyce/documents/ change.

The register of every requirement with its status and trace state. Open it from the Requirements tile or Noyce Compliance: Show Requirements Explorer. The register on the Canister firmware: 29 requirements, none trace-ready yet, so all 29 show as coverage gaps. The selected requirement's linked evidence is on the right. The counters at the top show requirements that are trace-ready, coverage gaps, and requirements with verified evidence. Select a requirement to see its rationale, its linked documents, the system requirement it traces to, and the code that implements it. Open in traceability map jumps to it in the graph. NoteExternal ALM tools such as Jama Connect and IBM DOORS Next are not connected; the view says so. Export from those tools to ReqIF or CSV and import the file in Requirements Authoring.

Write high-level requirements, import system requirements, and check them as you type. Open it with Noyce Compliance: Open Requirements Authoring. Requirements Authoring on the Canister copy: 17 high-level requirements in draft, each tracing up to a system requirement; 15 of them still have a lint error to fix. High-level requirements are written into the SRS document (SRS-001), so the document and the register never disagree. System requirements import from CSV, ReqIF, or a Markdown table. The imported file's hash is recorded, so you can show which version of the customer's requirements you worked from. The live check flags a requirement with two "shall"s, a TBD, or no parent, and will not let it be marked reviewed or baselined until it is fixed.

sections.h: Recover system requirements from a prototype
sections.t: When the firmware already works but its system requirements were never written down, run Noyce Compliance: Recover System Requirements from Prototype. Requirements Authoring opens with a Recovered from prototype section of candidate system requirements, read from the project's C sources and headers, STM32CubeMX .ioc files, and any interface control spreadsheets or CSVs. No model is involved: the same project always gives the same candidates. A candidate is only a proposal. Accept, edit or reject each one; an accepted candidate becomes a system requirement. Every decision is recorded in the audit trail with who made it, and the candidates and decisions are kept in .noyce/requirements/system-recovery.json.

Noyce IDE drafts low-level requirements from the code and shows every gap between functions, LLRs and HLRs. Open it with Noyce Compliance: Open Low-Level Requirements. Low-Level Requirements on the Canister copy before drafting: the gap counters across the top, and filters for drafts, accepted and rejected LLRs. Select Draft from code. Noyce IDE proposes one LLR per function from its signature, body and annotations and, when the reference manual is indexed, the registers it touches. No model is needed. Optionally select Draft intent with model to have your model state each function's required behaviour, and Suggest parents with model to propose the HLR each LLR refines. Review the drafts and accept or reject each one. A draft is only a draft. It counts as a low-level requirement once a person on your roster accepts it through a review record. Accepted LLRs are also what CBMC harnesses are generated from.

Lists every @req and @verification tag in the source. Run Noyce Compliance: Scan Workspace (⌘⌥N then S) to rescan, or open it with Open Annotation Navigator. Annotation Navigator: 20 tags on the Canister copy, each with its file, line and comment. Tag a requirement or a test in a comment: cCopy/* @req SYS-REQ-014: Forward auto-sequence with limit-switch gating */ /* @verification SYS-REQ-014: test_auto_seq_forward */ ImportantA requirement is labelled Verified only when it has an executed test result as evidence. A @verification tag that names a test does not make it evidence, so tagged requirements without a recorded test run read Needs review.

A live graph of requirements and what they link to: low-level requirements, source, tests, and design documents. Open it from its tile or Noyce Compliance: Open Traceability Graph. The Traceability Graph. Node colour shows the kind of item; the legend and filters are at the corners. The graph rebuilds by itself whenever the requirements or documents in .noyce/ change.

One view of everything Noyce IDE knows about the project: requirements, code, verification evidence, generated artifacts and objectives, with the links between them and any reference that points at nothing. Open it with Noyce Project Graph: Open Project Truth Graph. The Truth Graph for the Canister copy: 273 nodes and 607 edges, 29 requirements, and no unresolved references.
For the order to use these in, follow the DO-178C walkthrough. This page describes each surface.

The project's standing against a certification framework, objective by objective. Open it from the Compliance tile or ⌘⌥N then C. Compliance Evidence on the Canister copy at DAL A: 0 of 29 requirements linked, 1,532 analysis findings, 0% structural coverage, and 71 objectives with none satisfied. Header. Choose the framework (DO-178C, ISO 26262, IEC 62304 or IEC 61508) and the assurance level. The buttons along the top: Button Does Generate with AI Has your model draft the evidence for open objectives. Disabled until there are requirements. Generate via Orchestrator Puts each open objective on the Orchestrator board as a card. Generate All Evidence Runs every evidence producer the dashboard knows. Scan Rescans the project (⌘S inside the dashboard). Analysis Tools, Coupling, MC/DC Coverage Open those surfaces. Evidence Pack Writes a printable HTML evidence pack. Certification Package Writes the sealed package (below). JSON Exports the dashboard as JSON (⌘E). Body. Counters for requirements linked, design allocation, verification and analysis findings; the certification article with satisfied, partial, open and N/A counts; structural coverage against DO-178C A-7; and the objectives table, grouped by Annex A table, with each objective's reference, independence, status and the output it needs. Select an objective to open its drawer: the evidence behind it, Generate … with … for the agent that can produce it, its tool, and Review proposed evidence, where a reviewer from the roster accepts or rejects the evidence with a note. The drawer for A-1.1, "Software development and integral processes activities are defined": its output and independence, Generate Plan with Documentation Engineer, Generate via Orchestrator, and Open Annotation Navigator. NoteSet the assurance level here. The level in Settings has no effect. See Known limitations.

01EVIDENCE02MAPPING03REVIEW04STATUSProducer outputa run measured somethingProject-wide proxye.g. overall coverageAgent-drafted evidenceproposed, not countedmappedevery mapping records its basisObjective evidencethis objective's own kindsHuman reviewreviewer on rosteracceptedSatisfiedevidence + a personcan raise to partial, never to satisfiedPartialsome evidenceneeds a personAI reviewnever closes an objectivestaysOpennothing mapped yetFailinga mapped check failedIndependence is derived, not ticked: an agent, the author, or someone off the roster is never an independent reviewer. How an Annex A objective is graded. A producer's output, mapped to the objective with a stated basis, becomes that objective's evidence; only a review by a person on the roster makes it satisfied. A project-wide proxy can raise it to partial, never to satisfied, and an AI review never closes it. The grading is deliberately strict, so a green objective means the same thing to you and to an auditor: Only the objective's own evidence counts. A coverage objective reads coverage results, a review objective reads review records. A good number elsewhere in the project does not leak in. Proxies cap at partial. A project-wide measure, such as overall test coverage, can show progress but cannot satisfy a specific objective. A person closes it. The final step is always a review record by someone on the roster. Whether that review counts as independent is worked out from who wrote the item and who reviewed it. "Open" is not "failed". An objective with nothing mapped yet is open. It only shows as failing when a check mapped to it actually failed.

Expand Licensed Annex A table to import the applicability, independence and control category of each objective from your licensed copy of DO-178C. Write blank template creates the file to fill in. Until the table is imported, the PSAC, SVP, SCMP, SQAP and SAS stay marked DRAFT.

A reproducible measurement of the whole project at one commit. Open it from the Compliance Run tile or Noyce Compliance: Take a Compliance Run. Compliance Run before the first run: the DAL path lists each stage, from plans and standards to the summaries, with what it still needs. Take a run runs every evidence producer (static analysis, code scanning, formal verification, structural coverage and the rest) against the current configuration and stores the result under .noyce/compliance-runs/. Mark baseline fixes a run as the reference later runs are compared with. Annex A overlay sets up the objective map and objective text files. Objective map shows which producer discharges which objective. Map… assigns one; a mapping always records its basis. Each run shows its configuration, objectives by table, what each tool reported, conformity checks, the change since the previous run, and every run on record. A run cannot be exported when a producer failed, sample data was used, there is no commit, or the working tree has uncommitted changes.

Release blockers, weak evidence and next actions in one queue. Open it from the Readiness tile. Certification Readiness on the Canister copy: score 10, blocked by 16 critical blockers, with 0 of 29 requirements verified. The closure queue lists what to do next; the gap inspector explains each gap. Evidence that came from sample data is labelled inadmissible and never counts. The Security dimension runs its own CodeQL scan when the view refreshes, so its alert count can differ from Code Scanning, which shows only scans started from that view. A count is shown only when CodeQL really ran; otherwise the dimension says why it was not measured.

The project's process records. Open it from the Evidence Records tile. Each record type, its fields and the rules that make it count are described in Evidence records. Evidence Records: verification cases, problem reports, CCB, change sets, MISRA deviations, reviews, SQA / CM / liaison, roster, tool qualification and parameter data. Tab Holds Verification cases Test cases and their results. Problem reports Defects and change requests that authorise changes. CCB Change control board meetings, quorum and decisions. Change sets Proposed code changes awaiting gates and approval. See Review AI changes. MISRA deviations Approved deviations from MISRA rules. Reviews Review records with checklists. Independence is worked out from who wrote and who reviewed the item. SQA / CM / liaison Quality assurance, configuration management and certification liaison records. Roster The people who may review, approve and sign. Add everyone here first. Tool qualification The tools used and their qualification status. Parameter data Parameter data items.

Every significant action, recorded in a hash chain. Open it from the Audit Trail tile or Noyce Team: Open Audit Log. The audit trail on the Canister copy: each entry with its time, actor, action and hash. Chain integrity is checked on open; export as HTML or JSON. Each entry's hash covers its sequence number, time, actor, action and the previous entry's hash, so editing or removing any entry breaks the chain and the check reports where. The ledger is stored in .noyce/audit-ledger.json. Chain integrity is checked every time the ledger changes: Valid, or BROKEN @ #n at the first entry that does not verify. If this session failed to write an entry, a separate badge says how many events were not written. Filter by actor or by a single day. Agent actors are highlighted. Hash shows the first characters; select it to copy the full hash. Export HTML and Export JSON always contain the whole ledger, whatever the filters show, with the integrity result at the top of the HTML.

Evidence Pack on the Compliance Dashboard writes one printable HTML file to .noyce/compliance/exports/: totals for requirements, linked, orphaned and verified, the DO-178C Table A objectives with their status, the traceability matrix, and the MISRA findings. It is a readable snapshot for a review meeting; it carries no digest. For a sealed record, use the Certification Package.

Select Certification Package on the Compliance Dashboard. Noyce IDE runs CBMC and CodeQL, then writes one package to .noyce/certification/ as Markdown, HTML and JSON, with these sections: metadata, executive summary, objectives, Annex A coverage, compliance run identity, life-cycle data, requirements and traceability, MISRA, CBMC, CodeQL, review records, and the audit trail. The button is disabled until there are requirements and every objective has been assessed or reviewed, and the export is refused while the document set has unwaived contradictions. How the seal works. Each of the twelve sections is hashed with SHA-256. The package digest is a SHA-256 over every section's hash plus the current head of the audit trail, so it pins the package to the exact state of the ledger. The Markdown and HTML show the Package digest and the Audit-trail head; the HTML also shows whether the chain verified. The export itself is then recorded in the audit trail with the start of the digest. Open the result in the Document Reader; it renders the package as a formal document. WarningIf CBMC or CodeQL is not installed, the package fills those sections with seeded sample results and marks the package "WARNING: This package includes seeded sample data. It is NOT real evidence and cannot be used for certification." Install both tools before exporting a package you intend to submit. NoteThe package is sealed with SHA-256 hashes anchored to the audit trail, so later changes are detectable. It is not signed with a private key.

Every item in the project that is waiting on a person, in one list. Open it with Noyce Compliance: Open Review Inbox. Items are of three kinds: Supply (an input only you can give, such as a document's certification basis), Decide (a draft or proposal to accept or reject) and Sign (a review or approval the roster has to record). Blocking items come first, and Blocking only hides the rest. Select an item to open the surface where it is closed. The inbox reads the same records as those surfaces, so an item disappears as soon as it is closed anywhere.

Cyber Assurance, Data & Control Coupling, Object Code Traceability, MC/DC Coverage and Quality Trend are described in Analysis & proof. Review Workflow shows a requirement's linked evidence and its required sign-offs.

Evidence Records holds everything a certification authority asks you to show about how the software was built: who did what, which problems were raised and decided, which changes were authorised, and which reviews happened. Open it from its tile or Noyce Compliance: Open Evidence Records. Evidence Records has ten tabs, one per record type. Each is stored as a file in the project's .noyce folder. 01PEOPLE02AUTHORITY03CHANGE04WHAT IT CLOSESRosterpeople + rolesdeveloper · verifier · sqaconfiguration-managermanager · certification-liaisonProblem reportopen → in-work → closedCCB meetingquorum: 3, chair + SQAReview recordappended, never editeddecidesauthority: a PR or CCB decisionChange setauthority · gates · approveCode changedall files or noneindependent only if the roster says soAnnex A objectivereviewed evidenceSQA / CM recordsmade by the right roleApprovals, signatures, closures and CCB quorum are checked against the roster. With an empty roster they cannot be recorded, and no review counts as independent. Every record rests on the roster. Problem reports are decided at quorate CCB meetings and cited as the authority for a change set. Review records count as independent only through the roster, and SQA and configuration-management records close their objectives only when the right role made them. Two rules apply to every tab: Records that describe something that happened are append-only. Reviews, CCB minutes and SQA / CM records can be added but never edited; a mistaken SQA / CM record is voided with a reason and stays on file. Each form tells you whether the record will count. A box under the form says either "This record is complete and will count toward its objective" or lists why it will not count yet. NoteChecks in this view that depend on the software level, such as admissible verification cases and tool qualification levels, use the project's level. Verification-case independence is judged by the roster.

Roster lists the people who may author, review, approve, sign and attend meetings. Fill it in before anything else. The Roster on the Canister copy is empty, so independence, closure and quorum cannot yet be established for this project. Select Add person. Enter an Id (an employee id or email a record can cite), a Name and the Organisation. Choose one or more roles: developer, verifier, sqa, configuration-manager, manager, certification-liaison. Select Save. The roster refuses entries that would weaken the records: a person with no id or no name, a person with no role, a duplicate id, and any name that identifies an AI or a tool rather than a person. The roster decides: whether a review is independent, who may verify that a problem report is closed, who may attend, chair and act as SQA at a CCB meeting, and whether it was quorate, who may approve a change set or a MISRA deviation, who may make SQA and configuration-management records. NoteRemove asks you to confirm before deleting a person.

Defects, deficiencies and change requests, with their disposition. Open problem reports are what authorise a code change. Problem reports on the Canister copy: none raised yet. The header counts open, blocking and deferred reports. Select New report and fill in the Title, Raised by, Classification (requirement, design, code, verification, process or documentation), Severity and Description. An open blocking report stops a baseline. Lifecycle: open → in-work → resolved, deferred or closed. As a report moves on, more fields become required: To It needs Resolved A disposition: fix, defer or no-change. Deferred A rationale, a defer disposition, the safety effect, an AC/AMC 20-189 certification class, and a CCB decision to defer. A significant report cannot be deferred past certification. Closed A disposition, the certification class, the CCB decision, who implemented it, the changed configuration items for a fix, and Closure verified by: a person on the roster who is neither the implementer nor the person who dispositioned it. A closed or deferred report that fails these checks is not saved. Saved reports that later become inconsistent are badged incoherent in the list.

Change Control Board meetings and their decisions. A decision approves, rejects or defers the problem reports and change requests it names. The CCB tab. Record a meeting is disabled until the roster has people: attendees, chair and SQA are chosen from it. Select Record a meeting. Set the Meeting id, Date, the Attendees present, the Chair and the SQA (both chosen from the attendees). Add decision for each item: the subjects (for example PR-001, CR-002), the outcome (approve, reject or defer), the rationale, and a revisit date for a deferral. Write the Minutes and select Append minutes. A meeting is quorate with at least three attendees including a chair and an SQA representative, and the badge says quorum or why not. Minutes are appended, never rewritten, and are refused if a decision names no subject, has no rationale, or was taken without quorum.

Code changes proposed by agents and fixers, waiting for authority, gates and approval. They are created by Fix with Noyce, the CBMC and CodeQL fixers, the Firmware Validation Loop and Orchestrator agents, not in this tab. Change sets on the Canister copy: none staged. Generate portable build enables the build gate. The full workflow is in Review and apply AI changes. The authority you cite must be an open or in-work problem report, a change request approved by a quorate CCB decision, or that CCB decision itself. Until you select Generate portable build, the build gate is skipped.

Approved departures from a MISRA rule, with their scope and justification. Findings a deviation covers are counted as covered in the static-analysis results. MISRA deviations: import existing ones from docs/misra-deviations.md, or write a new one. Select New deviation, or Import from docs to read docs/misra-deviations.md and add each entry as proposed. Each deviation records the rule (or *), category, title, the files and lines or vendor folders it covers, the rationale, and a risk assessment with controls. Choose an Approver from the roster and select Approve. A mandatory guideline cannot be deviated, and an approver must be a person on the roster, never an AI. Editing an approved deviation sends it back to proposed.

Records of reviews that took place, with their checklist. Reviews are what close most Annex A objectives. Reviews on the Canister copy. Each was recorded by an AI on a person's behalf, so every one is marked not independent; none of them can close an objective that needs independence. Select Record a review, choose the Target (plan, standard, requirements, design, code, verification cases, verification results or configuration), name the item, the checklist, the Author of the item and the Reviewer, answer each checklist item, and set the outcome: accepted, accepted with actions, or rejected. Accepted with actions needs the problem reports it raised. Select Append. Independence is worked out, not ticked. A review is not independent when the reviewer or the author is an AI, when it is a self-review, when there is no roster, or when either person is not on it. The badge says independent or not independent with the reason.

Software quality assurance, configuration management and certification liaison records. Each kind closes specific objectives, but only when made by someone holding the matching role. Kind Role needed Closes SQA audit sqa A-9 (1–4), A-1 (6) Conformity review sqa A-9 (5) Configuration index configuration-manager A-8 (1) Release / archive configuration-manager A-8 (4) Load control configuration-manager A-8 (5) Environment control configuration-manager A-8 (6) Certification liaison certification-liaison A-10 (1–3) Select New record (it needs a roster), pick the kind, the person, the date, what it covers and a summary, then Record. Records are not edited; Void marks a mistaken one with who voided it and why.

The tool register: every tool used, the credit taken for it, and whether it needs qualification. Tool qualification on the Canister copy: the register is empty. Seed register adds the tools Noyce IDE itself uses. Seed register adds the tools Noyce IDE uses (the IDE itself, compiler, linker, CBMC, CodeQL, llvm-cov, the Unity runner and cppcheck), each with no credit taken. New tool adds another. For each, record the version, the executable's SHA-256, the credit taken (none, verification or development), the DO-330 criterion and, whenever credit is taken, the rationale. Qualification is required when credit is taken and the tool's output is not independently verified. The badge then shows the tool qualification level (TQL-1 to TQL-5) from the criterion and the software level, and asks for the qualification data.

Verification cases describe each test, analysis, review or inspection: the requirements it verifies, normal-range or robustness, the environment (target, simulator or host; only a target result discharges A-6(5)), the procedure, the expected result and, at Levels A and B, a reviewer other than the author. Parameter data lists each parameter data item with its file, SHA-256, description, requirements and how it was verified. A project with none can declare No parameter data with a statement and a plan reference.

Open DO-178C Documents from its tile or Noyce Compliance: Open DO-178C Documents. The library on the Canister copy: 17 documents at v1.0, none baselined yet, grouped by stage. The library holds the 17 DO-178C life-cycle documents: Group Documents Plans PSAC, SDP, SVP, SCMP, SQAP Standards SRSTD, SDSTD, SCSTD Core SRS, SDD, ICD, TRACE Verification SVCP, SVR Summary SECI, SCI, SAS Filter by group, search, sort by kind, and switch between Grid and List. Export all writes every document to Word; Regenerate stale re-authors documents whose workspace inputs have changed. Each card shows the document's revision, date and baseline state. Documents are stored as StrictDoc .sdoc files in .noyce/documents/, so they are plain text you can diff.
